title: Krishna's Verdict on Ashvatthama
story:
The son of Drona was brought in bound, and the camp came out to see him.

A night before, after the fighting had stopped, Ashvatthama had crept into the camp and killed the sleeping sons of Draupadi, wife of the Pandava brothers. Arjuna had hunted him down, and now he led him up with a rope about him, dragging him along like an animal. Ashvatthama's face was turned away, and even Arjuna, the man who had captured him, looked aside from his own errand in disgust. It was an uncomfortable sight for everyone: the warrior who had struck sleeping children by night, brought low at last before the very people he had wronged.

Bhima saw him and could not contain himself. "Do not spare him, Arjuna!" he cried. "This unworthy son of a brahmin — kill him! For what is he but the kind of man who would strike the mad, the careless, the sleeping, children, women, the helpless — who feeds his own life on the lives of others? Such a one is a cruel wretch, and his death is the only good thing left in him." And Bhima reminded them all of the promise. "You swore to Draupadi that you would bring her his head," he said, "and I was listening when you swore it. Let this sinner die — this assailant, this slayer of his own kindred."

Krishna heard it all — Bhima's fury and the vow he recalled, Draupadi's grief and what it demanded — and the tent waited for him to speak.

But Draupadi, who had more right than anyone to demand that death, could not bear the sight of him bound and dragged like cattle. She spoke, and her voice unsettled the certainties of the tent. Drona, she reminded them, had been the master of the secret science of weapons, the whole art of discharging them and calling them back; and that blessed teacher lived on, she said, in the form of his son. "Honor his family," she pleaded. "Let his mother Gautami, devoted as she is to her husband, not weep for this."

The tent fell into the silence of two truths pulling against each other. Nakula and Sahadeva, the two youngest of the five brothers, stood by; Satyaki, Krishna's own kinsman, waited with Arjuna; and Bhima, still burning, insisted that for such a man death itself was the only mercy. What was owed to the children who lay dead? What was owed to the mother who lived?

In that age the brahmin — the priest and teacher — was held sacred, and the law guarded even an unworthy son of such a house; yet the same law said that an assailant must not go free. Krishna held both truths in his hand. "A brahmin's unworthy son is not to be slain," he said, "yet an assailant deserves punishment. Both are my ordinances; uphold them. Keep the promise you made to your beloved, and satisfy Bhima, Panchali, and me." Panchali was Draupadi — so all called her, for the land of her father, the king of Panchala.

Arjuna understood what Krishna's heart intended. He stepped forward and, with his own hand, cut the jewel away from the head of Drona's son — the jewel along with the hair — so that the man who had thought to wear a warrior's glory walked away shorn and stripped of his treasure. Then Arjuna released him from his bonds and drove him from the camp.

The promise had asked for his head. What the camp saw was the jewel from that head, taken; the shaven scalp of a man who would never again be mistaken for a warrior; and a life, spared. The splendor of the child-killer was gone — the crime against sleeping children had stripped it from him.

The camp watched him go, and no one cheered. Bhima's fury had its answer, Draupadi's tears had theirs, and the vow that had sent Arjuna riding into the night had been kept in the one way that could answer everyone: a punishment that took everything but his life.
reflection: Krishna's judgment holds two ordinances together — the law that forbids slaying even an unworthy brahmin's son, and the law that an assailant must not go unpunished — and resolves them by making the punishment public and complete without making it fatal. The promise is kept in a way no one had imagined: not the head, but the honor the head carried, forfeited.
content_note: The episode turns on Ashvatthama's killing of the sleeping children, recalled without detail; his punishment is humiliation rather than violence.
next_story_tease: On the field where the war had ended, Bhishma still lay on his bed of arrows, waiting for the sun to turn north.
hero_scene: In the lamplit tent, Krishna stands between Bhima's fury and Draupadi's plea, one hand raised, while Arjuna kneels before the bound Ashvatthama, cutting the jewel away with a lock of his hair.
